1 Experimental Design

What is LARRY?

LARRY (Lineage And RNA RecoverY) is an expressed lentiviral barcode system that inserts a random 28-nucleotide barcode into cells. Because lentiviral integration is stable and heritable, all daughter cells carry the same barcode. This links a progenitor's transcriptional state to the differentiated fates of its clonal descendants.

Figure 1. Split-well experimental design. HSPCs are barcoded with LARRY, split into wells, and sequenced at days 4 (source) and 6 (target). Well 2 is held out as the test set.

Clone Selection Criteria (92 Test Clones)

  • Well 2 only -- held out from training, ensures unbiased evaluation
  • Present at both day 4 and day 6 -- enables source-to-target simulation
  • ≥20 cells at day 6 -- ensures W2 is well-estimated
  • <20% undifferentiated -- focuses on clones with clear fate commitment

Methods Evaluated

We benchmark 9 trajectory inference methods spanning ODE, SDE, flow matching, optimal transport, and PINN approaches:

2 The Per-Clone W2 Metric

Why Per-Clone W2?

Population-level W2 computes the distance between all simulated endpoints and all observed day-6 cells. A method can achieve good population W2 by "averaging" across fates -- e.g., placing simulated Neutrophil-fated cells halfway between Neutrophil and Monocyte regions. Per-clone W2 evaluates each clone individually: for clone b, it computes W2 between the simulated endpoints of clone b's day-4 cells and clone b's observed day-6 cells. This is a much more stringent test.

Figure 2. (a) Per-clone W2 measures the distance between simulated and observed distributions within each clone. (b) Population W2 can mask clone-specific failures -- a method may match the overall distribution while systematically misplacing specific clones. (c) Clone-size stratification: we split clones into small vs. large groups and compare W2 across groups.

Computation Details

  • Source cells: Clone b's cells at day 4
  • Simulation: Run the trained model's dynamics from day 4 to day 6
  • Target cells: Clone b's observed cells at day 6
  • W2 (raw): Wasserstein-2 distance in the original embedding space (DM10 or PC30), after inverse-standardizing if training used scaled data
  • Averaging: For methods with multiple seeds/runs, W2 is averaged per clone across runs

Figure 3. The hidden variable argument (Weinreb 2020). HSPCs carry heritable fate biases encoded in epigenomic, proteomic, and spatial properties that are invisible to scRNA-seq. The Data Processing Inequality proves these exist: late fate prediction is more accurate than early prediction, which is impossible if the transcriptome contains all fate-determining information. Per-clone W2 exposes the residual error caused by these unobserved variables.

3 Method Ranking

Experimental Design

For each of the 9 methods, we compute per-clone W2 for all 92 test clones, averaging across 3-4 seeds/runs. Methods are ranked by median per-clone W2 (robust to outliers). We show violin + strip + box plots to reveal the full distribution shape.

Two representation spaces:

  • DM10 -- 10-dimensional diffusion map embedding. Captures nonlinear manifold geometry; lower-dimensional.
  • PC30 -- 30-dimensional PCA embedding. Linear projection; higher-dimensional; preserves more variance.

Figure 4. Per-clone W2 distribution across 92 test clones for each method, ordered by median. Left: DM10 space. Right: PC30 space. Each point is one clone's average W2 across seeds.

Results

DM10: OTCFM achieves the lowest median per-clone W2 (0.00454), followed by SF2M (0.00517) and TrajectoryNet (0.00537). The top 7 methods are tightly clustered (0.0045-0.0059). MIOFlow (0.00678) and PRESCIENT (0.00749) trail.

PC30: scDiffEq leads (11.85), followed by DeepRUOT (12.34) and pdp+ (12.61). The spread is tighter: all 9 methods fall within 11.8-14.1.

Ranking flip: OTCFM ranks 1st in DM10 but 7th in PC30. scDiffEq ranks 4th in DM10 but 1st in PC30. Method performance is representation-dependent.

4 Biological Dissection

Experimental Design

We dissect per-clone W2 against five biological properties to understand what makes a clone hard to simulate. Analysis uses the best-performing method to isolate biology from method quality. Clone properties are computed from the h5ad file:

  • (a) Dominant fate: Most common non-undiff cell type at day 6
  • (b) Clone size: Number of cells at day 6
  • (c) Multipotency: Number of distinct non-undiff fate categories in the clone
  • (d) Pseudotime spread: Standard deviation of Palantir pseudotime at day 6 (within-clone differentiation variability)
  • (e) Initial state variance: Trace of day-4 covariance matrix (how spread-out the progenitors are)
  • (f) Method x fate heatmap: Median W2 broken down by method and dominant fate

Figure 5. Biological dissection in DM10 space.

Figure 6. Biological dissection in PC30 space.

Results

  • Multipotency correlates with difficulty (Spearman r ~ 0.43, p < 0.001). Clones with 3+ fates have systematically higher W2. This is consistent with the hidden variable hypothesis: multipotent clones make diverse fate choices driven by hidden factors that trajectory inference cannot model.
  • Pseudotime spread drives W2 (r ~ 0.48, p < 0.001). Clones with broader maturation ranges at day 6 are harder to simulate -- the within-clone stochastic variation in differentiation pace is not captured.
  • Megakaryocyte clones are 2-2.6x harder across all methods. Meg fate arises via a "direct route" from LT-HSCs that bypasses standard multipotent intermediates (Rodriguez-Fraticelli 2018). Most methods are not designed for this non-canonical trajectory.

Implications

The difficulty hierarchy is biological, not algorithmic. No current method -- whether ODE or SDE -- overcomes the fundamental limitation that heritable fate biases are invisible to the transcriptome. Future methods incorporating epigenomic (e.g., ReDeeM mitochondrial mutations) or chromatin accessibility data may close this gap.

5 Clone-Size Stratified Analysis

Experimental Design

Do methods perform differently on large vs. small clones? We split the 92 test clones into two groups by day-6 clone size and compare per-clone W2 distributions. Potential confounds:

  • Large clones have more cells -> W2 is better estimated (lower sampling noise)
  • Large clones may have different fate compositions (proliferation bias, Bonham-Carter 2024)
  • Small clones may be more fate-restricted (fewer cells -> less diversity)

We sweep the cutoff to test robustness: if a pattern holds across cutoffs, it reflects biology rather than a single arbitrary threshold.

Figure 7. Top: Ratio of median W2 (large/small group) across cutoff values for each method. Values above 1.0 mean large clones are harder. Bottom: Grouped bar chart at the median clone size cutoff.

Figure 8. Box plots of per-clone W2 for small vs. large clone groups at each cutoff (all methods pooled). Shows how the group distributions shift as the cutoff changes.

Results

DM10: Large clones (n>22) have median W2 = 0.006176 vs small clones (n<=22) median W2 = 0.005608 (ratio = 1.10, Mann-Whitney p = 0.0037). N = 45 large, 47 small clones.

PC30: Large clones (n>22) have median W2 = 13.630372 vs small clones (n<=22) median W2 = 13.256033 (ratio = 1.03, Mann-Whitney p = 0.0306). N = 45 large, 47 small clones.

Implications

Clone size stratification disentangles two factors: (1) statistical power (large clones give more reliable W2 estimates) and (2) biological complexity (large clones may have more diverse fate outcomes due to longer proliferative history). If large clones consistently show higher W2, it suggests that proliferative clones -- which dominate the dataset due to growth bias -- are also biologically harder to simulate.

6 Sensitivity Analysis

Experimental Design

We test how method ranking changes when we vary the minimum clone size filter. Starting from our baseline of ≥20 cells, we sweep thresholds from 5 to 50 cells. This reveals:

  • Whether rankings are robust to the inclusion/exclusion of small clones
  • Whether any method is artificially helped by small-clone sampling noise
  • The trade-off between clone count (statistical power) and per-clone W2 reliability

Figure 9. Sensitivity analysis in DM10.

Figure 10. Sensitivity analysis in PC30.

Results

Method rankings are broadly stable across clone size thresholds. In DM10, OTCFM remains the top performer at all thresholds. In PC30, scDiffEq consistently leads. The relative ordering between the mid-pack methods may shift at extreme thresholds (n≥50), but this is driven by few remaining clones (<20) rather than meaningful biological signal.

7 Statistical Tests

Experimental Design

We use paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to assess whether the per-clone W2 differences between methods are statistically significant. The test is paired because each clone is evaluated by all methods -- the same 92 clones form natural pairs. Bonferroni correction is applied for 36 pairwise comparisons (9 methods choose 2).

The heatmap shows -log10(p) values (Bonferroni-corrected) in the color scale, with raw corrected p-values as annotations. Higher -log10(p) = more significant difference.

Figure 11. Paired Wilcoxon heatmap, DM10.

Figure 12. Paired Wilcoxon heatmap, PC30.

Results

In DM10, the top cluster (OTCFM, SF2M, TrajectoryNet, scDiffEq, DeepRUOT, pdp+, TIGON) is not always significantly different from each other after Bonferroni correction. However, MIOFlow and PRESCIENT are significantly worse than most methods (p < 0.05). In PC30, the spread is tighter and fewer pairwise comparisons reach significance.

Key Takeaways

Main Findings

  1. Per-clone W2 is more discriminating than population W2. All methods cluster tightly at the population level; per-clone analysis reveals a wider spread and more nuanced ranking.
  2. Rankings are representation-dependent. OTCFM excels in DM10 (10D manifold) while scDiffEq leads in PC30 (30D linear). No single method dominates across both spaces.
  3. Difficulty is biological. Multipotent clones, Meg-fated clones, and clones with high pseudotime spread are systematically harder for all methods. This correlates with the hidden variable argument (Weinreb 2020).
  4. SDE does not help with multipotent clones. Stochastic methods do not outperform deterministic methods on high-multipotency clones (ratio ~ 1.06). The residual error is not noise that can be modeled by adding Brownian motion.
  5. Results are robust to clone size filtering. Method rankings are stable across minimum clone size thresholds from 5 to 50 cells.

Looking Forward

Per-clone W2 reveals a floor that no current transcriptomics-only method can break through. Clones whose fates are driven by hidden variables (epigenomic, proteomic, spatial) will always have high per-clone W2 when simulated from scRNA-seq alone. Future trajectory inference methods should incorporate multi-omic measurements (SHARE-seq, ReDeeM, CITE-seq) to capture these hidden determinants. The per-clone W2 metric provides a direct way to measure progress toward this goal.
